title: Mode
summary: The mode is a most frequent sample value, or a maximiser of a pmf or a pdf. A distribution may have more than one mode, and the mode need not equal the mean.
intuition:
The mode answers a different question from the mean. It asks which value is most common, not where the probability-weighted balance point sits. In a sample, count the repetitions. A value that appears strictly more often than every other value is the unique sample mode. If two values tie for the highest count, the sample is multimodal and both values are modes.

For a discrete distribution the same idea is applied to the pmf. A mode is any point $x$ at which $p(x)$ attains its maximum. The height $p(x)$ has to be the largest height; a value with a large label and a small probability is not the mode. For a density, a mode is a maximiser of $f$. It can sit at an endpoint. The density $f(x)=2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ decreases from $f(0)=2$ to $f(1)=0$, so its mode is 0, while its mean is $1/3$.

Nothing forces uniqueness. A pmf that puts probability $7/20$ on both 1 and 2, and less on the neighbouring points, has two modes. The mean of that distribution is $3/2$, which is not either mode. Saying 'the mode' as if there were always one, or replacing it by the mean, changes the summary.

definitions.body: A value that attains the highest frequency in a finite sample. If several values share that highest frequency, each of them is a mode and the sample is multimodal.
A point $x$ in the support such that $p(x)\ge p(t)$ for every $t$. Equivalently, $x$ is an argmax of the probability mass function.

A point at which the density attains its maximum. A continuous distribution is multimodal when the density has two or more separated maxima of equal height, or more generally more than one local maximum that the problem calls a mode.

formulas.name: Discrete mode
formulas.note: Every maximiser is a mode. The maximal probability itself is not the mode; the mode is the $x$ that achieves it.

formulas.name: Continuous mode
formulas.note: Maximise the density, not the cdf. The median equation $F(m)=1/2$ is a different summary.

properties: A distribution can have more than one mode. The pmf with masses $3/20,7/20,7/20,3/20$ on $0,1,2,3$ has modes at 1 and at 2.
The mode is not the mean. That pmf has mean $3/2$, which is not a mode, and $f(x)=2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ has mode 0 and mean $1/3$.
The mode is not the largest value in the support unless that largest value also has the largest probability or density.
For a sample, frequencies are counts of equal values. A value that occurs once is not the mode when another value occurs three times, however large the singleton is.
Shifting a random variable by a constant $c$ shifts every mode by $c$. The heights of the pmf or pdf do not change.

examples.title: A sample whose mode is not its mean
examples.prompt: Find the mode of the sample 4, 7, 4, 9, 4, 7, 2, 4, and compare it with the sample mean.
steps: Count the values. The number 4 appears four times, 7 appears twice, and 9 and 2 appear once each.
The unique highest frequency is 4, so the sample mode is 4.
The sum of the eight observations is $4+7+4+9+4+7+2+4=41$, so the mean is $41/8$. Since $41/8\neq 4$, the mode and the mean are different.
examples.answer: The mode is 4, and the mean is $41/8$.

examples.title: A pmf with two modes
examples.prompt: The pmf of $X$ is $P(X=0)=3/20$, $P(X=1)=7/20$, $P(X=2)=7/20$, and $P(X=3)=3/20$. Find the modes and the mean.
steps: The four probabilities sum to 1, and the largest height is $7/20$.
That height is attained at both $x=1$ and $x=2$, so both points are modes. The distribution is bimodal.
The mean is $0\cdot(3/20)+1\cdot(7/20)+2\cdot(7/20)+3\cdot(3/20)=7/20+14/20+9/20=30/20=3/2$. The mean $3/2$ is not equal to either mode.
examples.answer: The modes are 1 and 2. The mean is $3/2$, which is not a mode.

examples.title: A density whose mode is an endpoint
examples.prompt: The density $f(x)=2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$, and $f(x)=0$ elsewhere, decreases from 2 to 0. Find a mode and the mean.
steps: On $[0,1]$ the derivative is $f'(x)=-2<0$, so the maximum is at the left endpoint. The mode is $x=0$, where $f(0)=2$.
The mode 0 and the mean $1/3$ are different numbers. The median would solve $F(m)=1/2$ and is a third summary, not this argmax.
examples.answer: The mode is 0 and the mean is $1/3$.

traps: Reporting the largest observation as the mode. In the sample 4, 7, 4, 9, 4, 7, 2, 4 the largest observation is 9, and the mode is 4.
Averaging two modes and calling the average the mode. The bimodal pmf has modes 1 and 2; the midpoint $3/2$ is the mean, and $p(3/2)$ is not even defined on this support.
Equating the mode with the mean. The density $f(x)=2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ has mode 0 and mean $1/3$.
Maximising the cdf instead of the pmf or pdf. The cdf is nondecreasing, so its maximum is at the right endpoint and does not locate the mode.
python:
from fractions import Fraction
sample = [4, 7, 4, 9, 4, 7, 2, 4]
mode = max(set(sample), key=sample.count)
assert mode == 4 and sample.count(4) == 4
assert sum(sample) == 41
probs = {0: Fraction(3, 20), 1: Fraction(7, 20), 2: Fraction(7, 20), 3: Fraction(3, 20)}
assert sum(probs.values()) == 1
top = max(probs.values())
assert sorted(x for x, p in probs.items() if p == top) == [1, 2]
mean = sum(x * p for x, p in probs.items())
assert mean == Fraction(3, 2)
# mean of f(x)=2(1-x) on [0,1] is 1/3; mode is the left endpoint
assert 2 * (Fraction(1, 2) - Fraction(1, 3)) == Fraction(1, 3)
print(4, float(mean))

questions.stem: The mode of the sample 5, 1, 5, 8, 5, 1 is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $5$.

The value 5 appears three times, 1 appears twice, and 8 appears once. The unique mode is 5. Option D is the mean $(5+1+5+8+5+1)/6=25/6$, which is not a value in the sample and is not the mode. Option C is the largest observation.

questions.stem: A pmf satisfies $P(X=2)=1/10$, $P(X=5)=3/5$, and $P(X=8)=3/10$. The mode is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $5$.

Compare the probabilities: $3/5=0.6$ is larger than $3/10$ and larger than $1/10$, so the unique mode is 5. Option D is the mean $2(1/10)+5(3/5)+8(3/10)=1/5+3+12/5=28/5$, which is not the argmax of the pmf. Option B picks the largest support point instead of the largest probability.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: A mode of a pmf is a value $x$ that maximises $p(x)$.
A distribution can have two modes.
The mode equals the mean for every distribution.
A mode of a pdf is a point at which the density attains its maximum.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

A and D are the argmax definitions for a mass function and a density. B is witnessed by the pmf with masses $3/20$, $7/20$, $7/20$, and $3/20$, whose modes are 1 and 2. C fails for that pmf, whose mean is $3/2$, and it also fails for $f(x)=2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$, whose mode is 0 and whose mean is $1/3$.

questions.stem: Enter the mode of the sample 3, 3, 6, 3, 6, 9, 3.
questions.solution:
The answer is **3**.

The value 3 appears four times, 6 appears twice, and 9 appears once. The unique highest frequency belongs to 3, so the mode is 3. The largest observation is 9, and it is not the mode.

questions.stem: A pmf satisfies $P(X=1)=1/5$, $P(X=4)=1/2$, and $P(X=7)=3/10$. Enter the mode.
questions.solution:
The answer is **4**.

The probabilities are $1/5=0.2$, $1/2=0.5$, and $3/10=0.3$. The unique maximum is $1/2$, attained at $x=4$. The mean is $1(1/5)+4(1/2)+7(3/10)=1/5+2+21/10=43/10$, which is not the mode.
